newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australia sugar output, exports to rise - ABARE.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australia sugar output, exports to rise - ABARE.

text.p: Australian raw sugar production is forecast to rise to 5.45 million tonnes 94 net titre in 1997/98 (July-June) from 5.32 million tonnes in 1996/97, the Australian Bureau of Agricultural and Resource Economics (ABARE) said in Tuesday.
ABARE also forecast a rise in Australian sugar export volume and value in 1997/98, it said in its latest Australian Commodities quarterly.
It forecast 1997/98 sugar exports would rise to 4.60 million tonnes worth an estimated A$1.47 billion from 4.25 million tonnes worth A$1.42 billion in 1996/97.
ABARE said the forecast 2.5 percent rise in raw sugar output reflected an expected increase in land assignments in Queensland, the main sugar producing state.

"Despite the rise in export value, the gross value of cane production is forecast to fall because the expansion in Australian sugar production is expected to be less than the decline in world sugar prices in 1997/98," it said.
Average returns to Australian sugar producers were forecast to decline by five percent, in line with the forecast fall in world sugar prices, it said.
The 1996/97 cane crop was crushed over June-December 1996.
Turning to the world outlook, ABARE said world raw sugar prices are forecast to fall to an average 10.3 U.S. cents a pound in 1997/98 from 10.8 cents in 1996/97.
"While the forecast represents a most likely outcome, there is a 75 percent probability of the final outcome being in the range 9.6-11.8 U.S. cents a pound," it said.

After falling to 123 million tonnes in 1996/97 from 126 million in 1995/96, world sugar production is forecast to rise slightly to 124 million tonnes in 1997/98, mainly because of increased output in Latin America and India, ABARE said.
In Cuba, for example, production is likely to increase in 1997/98 after Hurricane Lili reduced the previous crop, ABARE said.
India's production is forecast to increase slightly in 1997/98 as yields recover from the low levels of 1996/97.
The Indian government will still fix an export ceiling which will limit any increase in sugar exports, despite some liberalisation of sugar trade restrictions in India, it said.
